topic: Where do the heavy elements in the universe come from? The origins of heavy elements (which have an atomic  number of 92 or higher) and superheavy elements (with  an atomic number of at least 112) are still somewhat of  a mystery to scientists. We have been able to produce  some heavy elements in experiments that take place  in reactors, and artificially produce heavy elements in  cyclotrons. But beyond those produced on terra firma,  what is the origin story of heavy elements? We turn to astrophysics for our answer. We know  that the light elements, such as hydrogen, helium, and  lithium, were formed at the dawn of the universe by the  Big Bang. Elements as heavy as iron (atomic number  26) are the product of fusion in the cores of stars. The  higher the atomic number, the more force is needed  to create the element, and indeed, gallium (31) and  bromine (35) need a huge celestial event, such as a  supernova. Another astrophysical process, the rapid  neutron-capture process (r-process), entails neutrons  being quickly added to an atom’s nucleus; this process  is responsible for many of the elements heavier than  iron, such as gold and uranium.    One potential source for heavy elements was recently  confirmed: In 2019, an international team of researchers  reported that neutron stars may be a significant  source. The scientists examined a kilonova (neutron  star merger) 140 million light-years from Earth, which  they were able to observe through the detection of the  merger’s gravitational waves. What they saw was incredibly exciting. As Science  reporter Daniel Clery notes, “Computer modeling  revealed that strontium [atomic number 38] in  the expanding ball of gas would absorb light at  wavelengths of 350 and 850 nanometers. When they  looked again at the X-shooter spectra, they found dips  in the spectra at those wavelengths. The end result: five  Earth masses worth of strontium.” The presence of strontium confirms that heavy  elements are created by neutron star mergers and  other cataclysmic astrophysical events. The work was  additionally important because it marked the first time  that scientists were able to see an individual element in  a kilonova’s aftermath.

directions.title: Fission Fragment Precursor Formalism: Beta-Decay Neutron Release Timing as a Necessary Condition for r-Process Fission Cycling in Neutron Star Mergers
directions.abstract: The origin of heavy elements via the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) in neutron star mergers remains incompletely understood, particularly the role of fission cycling in the dynamical ejecta. We formalize the treatment of r-process fission cycling by applying the reactor kinetics concept of the effective neutron multiplication factor ($k_{eff}$). Rather than treating fission merely as a termination step, we derive a precise criticality condition for the dynamical ejecta: sustained fission cycling requires the prompt neutron multiplication factor to exceed unity ($k_{eff} > 1$), balancing prompt fission neutron yield against expansion and parasitic capture losses. This formal relation predicts observable spectral and kinematic signatures distinguishing fission-driven cycling in dynamical ejecta from single-pass nucleosynthesis in alternative sites or secular ejecta, providing a rigorous theoretical framework connecting terrestrial reactor criticality physics to astrophysical heavy element synthesis.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Sustained r-process fission cycling in the dynamical ejecta of neutron star mergers requires the effective neutron multiplication factor ($k_{eff}$) of prompt fission neutrons to strictly exceed unity, overcoming losses due to geometric expansion and parasitic neutron capture, a condition not required for single-pass nucleosynthesis in alternative sites.
hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: The prompt neutron yield per fission event must exceed the combined neutron loss rates from expansion and parasitic capture, establishing a critical neutron multiplication threshold ($k_{eff} > 1$) for fission cycling sustainability.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Relax the qualitative assumption that fission merely terminates the r-process, replacing it with a formal criticality condition derived from mapping the reactor kinetics effective multiplication factor ($k_{eff}$) to the astrophysical r-process environment in the dynamical ejecta.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: By mapping the reactor kinetics concept of $k_{eff}$ to the astrophysical r-process in the dynamical ejecta, the formalism mathematically couples the prompt fission neutron multiplicity to the local neutron density and expansion rate, dictating whether the fission cycle can overcome losses and sustain the r-process.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Observable spectral and kinematic signatures in kilonova ejecta, specifically requiring the isolation of the lanthanide-rich dynamical ejecta component via its distinct expansion velocity and opacity, to measure the abundance ratios of third r-process peak elements versus lighter fission products and distinguish sustained cycling from single-pass or non-cycling alternatives.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Verification of the critical neutron multiplication threshold through comparison with observed kilonova spectral abundances in the isolated dynamical ejecta component, and sensitivity analysis against theoretical nuclear mass models.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Theoretical nuclear mass models, prompt fission neutron multiplicities, and cross-sections for neutron-rich nuclei near the drip line, combined with kinematically resolved kilonova spectral observations.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The formalism fails and the zero-dimensional point-kinetics approximation breaks down when spatial and temporal gradients in neutron density and temperature within the expanding dynamical ejecta exceed the local mixing timescale, defining the counterexample_boundary.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Applies specifically to the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) in the high-entropy, extremely neutron-rich dynamical ejecta of neutron star mergers, distinguishing it from secular ejecta and alternative astrophysical sites where single-pass nucleosynthesis or non-cycling fission termination may dominate.

directions.title: Kinematic Decoupling of Fission Recycling in Kilonovae: A Delayed Neutron Release Mechanism for Third r-Process Peak Shifts and Anisotropic Curtaining
directions.abstract: We propose that the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) in neutron star mergers is fundamentally limited not by thermodynamics, but by the kinematic timescale of beta-delayed and isomer-delayed fission neutron release. By inverting the standard assumption of instantaneous fission equilibrium, we derive a formal relation where the delayed fission timescale competes with relativistic ejecta expansion. This mechanism modifies the freeze-out abundance distribution of the third r-process peak and actinides, and induces viewing-angle-dependent lanthanide curtaining. Crucially, we construct the specific temporal evolution of actinide spectral absorption signatures that discriminate this fission-driven decoupling from alternative geometric or magnetic asymmetry confounders, providing a unified framework for multi-messenger progenitor decoupling.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The kinematic delay in beta-delayed and isomer-delayed fission neutron release relative to ejecta expansion formally unifies the modification of the third r-process peak freeze-out abundance with viewing-angle-dependent lanthanide curtaining, producing a distinct temporal evolution of actinide spectral lines that cannot be replicated by purely geometric or magnetic ejecta asymmetries.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Delayed neutron release from beta-decaying and isomer-trapped superheavy nuclei decouples the late-stage r-process from the prompt relativistic outflow, spatially segregating actinides and altering the opacity evolution to produce anisotropic spectral absorption features, specifically in actinide lines, which are insensitive to pure geometric ejecta asymmetries.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Viewing-angle-dependent temporal evolution of specific actinide spectral absorption features, which diverge from both instantaneous recycling models and purely geometric/magnetic asymmetry confounders.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Spectroscopic identification of the temporal evolution of viewing-angle-dependent actinide lines in multi-messenger kilonova observations, strictly inconsistent with both instantaneous fission equilibrium and pure geometric asymmetry models.

hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mechanism fails if the effective fission timescale for superheavy nuclei is strictly shorter than the expansion timescale, or if geometric/magnetic asymmetries alone can perfectly replicate the predicted actinide spectral shifts without invoking delayed fission timescales.

directions.abstract: The origins of superheavy elements (Z ≥ 112) and the precise positioning of the third r-process peak (A ≈ 195) remain constrained by the assumption of instantaneous fission recycling in neutron star mergers. By replacing the instantaneous recycling axiom with a delayed fission neutron release derivation, we establish a unified mechanism linking fission dynamics to observable kilonova spectral signatures. Crucially, we isolate this effect from confounding variations in bulk ejecta properties, providing a falsifiable boundary condition that discriminates fission-driven nucleosynthesis from standard beta-decay-dominated scenarios.

directions.title: Delayed Neutron Precursor Formalism for r-Process Fission Cycling: Beta-Decay Timing as the Control Parameter for Recycling Efficiency
directions.abstract: Standard simplified r-process nucleosynthesis models and computationally constrained hydrodynamic couplings often assume instantaneous fission recycling, treating fission fragments as immediate neutron sources. We relax this assumption by importing the delayed neutron precursor formalism from nuclear reactor kinetics: fission fragments produced during r-process cycling are treated as precursors whose beta-decay half-lives determine the timescale and efficiency of neutron re-release. We derive the modified fission cycling equations with time-dependent neutron source terms and establish the validity domain for this precursor-based formalism. This framework provides a rigorous, computationally efficient analytical alternative to full time-dependent network calculations, predicting systematic shifts in third r-process peak abundances that discriminate time-dependent fission-driven recycling from instantaneous approximations.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: Treating r-process fission fragments as delayed neutron precursors whose beta-decay half-lives govern recycling efficiency in simplified or parameterized r-process models produces systematically different third r-process peak abundance patterns compared to instantaneous recycling approximations, with the shift magnitude scaling with the mean fragment decay timescale relative to the astrophysical expansion timescale, offering a computationally efficient alternative to full time-dependent network calculations.

scientific_object.description: fission_precursor_formalism: a formal treatment of r-process fission fragments as delayed neutron precursors whose beta-decay timing controls recycling efficiency, serving as a computationally efficient analytical proxy for full time-dependent network calculations

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: decay_timing_efficiency_relation: the formal relation mapping fission fragment beta-decay half-life distributions to effective r-process fission cycling rate and recycling efficiency in parameterized models.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Relax the standard instantaneous fission recycling assumption in simplified models by constructing the fission_precursor_formalism, replacing prompt neutron release with time-delayed beta-decay neutron source terms derived from fragment precursor decay chains.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: The delayed precursor formalism introduces a characteristic timescale into fission cycling: fragments must beta-decay before releasing neutrons or returning to the capture path, creating a bottleneck that reduces effective recycling efficiency during rapid expansion. This time-dependent neutron availability shifts the freeze-out conditions, altering the final abundance distribution—particularly enhancing or suppressing third-peak elements (A~195) relative to lighter r-process products.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Comparison of predicted abundance ratios (e.g., Au/Pt, rare-earth peak to third-peak ratio) from the precursor-based formalism against instantaneous recycling approximations and full time-dependent network calculations, tested against kilonova spectral observations such as the strontium detection and lanthanide/actinide signatures in GW170817.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Derived abundance patterns from the modified fission cycling equations must reproduce observed r-process residuals in metal-poor stars and kilonova spectra, specifically matching the third-peak position and width within observational uncertainties, while demonstrating computational efficiency and accuracy comparable to full time-dependent network calculations.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Derived abundance patterns from modified fission cycling equations; comparison with kilonova spectral observations (strontium detection in GW170817); consistency with r-process residuals in metal-poor stellar spectra; benchmarking against full time-dependent network calculations.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The precursor formalism becomes invalid when: (1) fragment beta-decay half-lives greatly exceed the astrophysical expansion timescale (t_exp < 10 ms), causing fission neutrons to be lost to expansion before capture; (2) temperatures exceed ~10 GK where photodisintegration dominates over beta-decay, breaking the precursor analogy; (3) neutron densities drop below ~10^20 cm^-3 where neutron capture competes poorly with decay. These conditions define the counterexample_boundary.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Applicable to simplified analytical models, parameterized network studies, and computationally constrained hydrodynamic couplings of r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star merger ejecta, specifically for evaluating time-dependent fission cycling effects on elements beyond the second r-process peak (A>130) without the computational cost of full time-dependent network calculations.
assumptions: Fission fragment beta-decay half-lives follow systematics extrapolated from known nuclei; the precursor analogy holds when decay timescales are comparable to or shorter than expansion timescales; photodisintegration rates are subdominant to beta-decay in the relevant temperature regime; the formalism serves as an efficient analytical proxy for full time-dependent network calculations rather than replacing them in high-fidelity simulations.

directions.falsifier: If the derived abundance patterns from the precursor-based formalism fail to match the results of full time-dependent network calculations within the defined validity domain, or if the predicted shifts in third-peak abundances are not observable in high-resolution kilonova spectra or metal-poor stellar abundances, the formalism is falsified as a useful analytical proxy.

directions.title: Fission-Driven Neutron Release and Third r-Process Peak Shifts in Kilonova Spectra
directions.abstract: We address the evidence role deficit in kilonova viewing-angle dependencies and the unmapped gap in relativistic outflow phenomena by unifying them under a shared fission-driven neutron release mechanism. By replacing the weak assumption of instantaneous fission recycling with a refined derivation linking fission neutron release timescales to third r-process peak abundance shifts, we construct a formal mechanism that admits both geometric and dynamical constraints. This mechanism construction restricts the validity domain to kilonova spectra conditioned on initial electron fraction (Ye) and 3D geometry, predicting specific spectral absorption signatures that discriminate fission-driven nucleosynthesis from alternative Ye-driven or alpha-rich freeze-out scenarios.

directions.title: Time-Dependent Fission Cycling and the Third r-Process Peak Shift in Kilonova Ejecta
directions.abstract: The origin of the heaviest elements via the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) in neutron star mergers relies on fission cycling, yet standard analytical models often assume instantaneous fission recycling. We relax the instantaneous fission recycling axiom, replacing it with a time-dependent fission neutron yield derivation. By unifying the relativistic outflow dynamics with heavy element target constraints, we establish a shared nucleosynthesis mechanism and derive the explicit functional relationship between fission neutron release timescales and the shift of the third r-process peak (A~195). This formal construction defines the kilonova ejecta validity domain, explicitly bounded by a counterexample boundary where initial electron fraction and entropy variations perfectly mimic the peak shift, and provides observable signatures to discriminate fission-driven nucleosynthesis from alternative scenarios.

directions.title: Formalizing R-Process Fission Cycling: Deriving the Timing-Efficiency Coupling Relation from Delayed Neutron Precursor Formalism
directions.abstract: The origin of heavy elements via the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) relies on fission cycling, yet the assumption that fission fragments act simply as delayed neutron precursors lacks a rigorous mathematical foundation in expanding ejecta. We replace this weak assumption with a formal derivation of r-process fission cycling dynamics within a Lagrangian comoving frame, explicitly constructing the timing-efficiency coupling relation. By treating fission fragments as precursors whose beta-decay neutron release timing mathematically dictates local recycling efficiency, we establish a rigorous point-kinetics formalism for subcritical astrophysical environments. This refined derivation provides a falsifiable boundary for the validity of the comoving point-kinetics analogy, formally bounding the third r-process peak abundance shift when alternative mechanisms like global hydrodynamic mixing are subdominant.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The beta-decay neutron release timing of r-process fission fragments mathematically dictates the local neutron recycling efficiency within a comoving fluid element, formally analogous to delayed neutron precursors in point-kinetics; within the validity domain where global hydrodynamic mixing and initial seed distribution variations are subdominant, this local coupling formally bounds the maximum achievable abundance shift of the third r-process peak prior to expansion dilution.

directions.title: Formal Derivation of Anisotropic Neutrino-Irradiation Fission Sorting in Kilonova Ejecta
directions.abstract: We propose a formal derivation of the shared kilonova nucleosynthesis mechanism that replaces the assumption of uniform thermodynamic trajectories with a spatially anisotropic construction linking central remnant neutrino flux gradients to electron fraction ($Y_e$) and entropy stratification. By unifying joint spectral and gravitational constraints, we resolve the evidence deficit in viewing-angle dependencies and map neutrino-driven fission cycling to observable multi-messenger signatures, explicitly bounding this mechanism against competing magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) wind contributions to isolate the neutrino-driven component.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The joint spectral and gravitational constraints formally admit the shared kilonova nucleosynthesis mechanism if and only if the electron fraction ($Y_e$) and entropy stratification are derived from the anisotropic neutrino irradiation of a surviving central remnant—distinct from and bounded against magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) wind contributions—which governs the spatial distribution of fission cycling and the resulting heavy element abundance peaks.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Relax the uniform thermodynamic trajectory assumption and construct a spatially anisotropic derivation linking central remnant neutrino flux gradients to $Y_e$- and entropy-dependent fission cycling, while formally bounding the derivation to isolate neutrino-driven effects from magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) wind and shock-heating mechanisms.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Anisotropic neutrino irradiation from the hypermassive neutron star remnant creates a polar-equatorial $Y_e$ and entropy gradient. This gradient determines the local neutron-to-seed ratio and the onset of fission cycling, sorting the final r-process abundance patterns (including heavy and superheavy elements) by angle and driving viewing-angle dependent spectral absorption, independent of MHD-driven anisotropies.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Observation of viewing-angle dependent spectral absorption dips (lanthanide curtaining) and corresponding gravitational wave phase shifts that uniquely require anisotropic $Y_e$ and entropy gradients to reproduce the observed heavy element abundance peaks, after marginalizing over MHD wind parameters.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Proof or verification that the anisotropic neutrino-driven fission cycling derivation uniquely reproduces the observed 3D spectral absorption dips and viewing-angle light curve variations when MHD wind parameters are marginalized, falsifiable via the neutrino anisotropy ablation.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The claim holds within the kilonova ejecta validity domain where the central remnant survives long enough to emit anisotropic neutrinos and where MHD wind contributions are formally bounded; it fails if the remnant collapses promptly to a black hole, or if MHD winds dominate the $Y_e$ gradient generation, eliminating the unique neutrino-driven signature.

directions.title: Delayed Fission Neutron Release Timescales and Third r-Process Peak Shifts in Kilonova Outflows
directions.abstract: The origin of the heaviest r-process elements (actinides and fission-barrier nuclei) in neutron star mergers remains constrained by unresolved phenomenological gaps in relativistic outflow decoupling. We replace the standard assumption of instantaneous fission feedback with a formal derivation of the delayed fission neutron release timescale. By unifying this timescale with the third r-process peak shift, we establish a target relation that discriminates fission-driven nucleosynthesis from alternative scenarios. We prove that this mechanism satisfies the joint constraints of multi-messenger progenitor decoupling and actinide abundances, bounded by high-entropy ejecta validity domains and explicitly isolated from initial electron fraction and entropy variations, and verified against kilonova spectral synthesis.

hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Replace the instantaneous_fission_feedback_assumption with the delayed_fission_neutron_release_timescale_derivation, explicitly bounding the validity domain against initial electron fraction and entropy variations.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: The finite timescale of fission neutron injection delays the secondary r-process cycling, altering the final abundance distribution and shifting the third r-process peak relative to instantaneous feedback models, thereby governing the termination of the r-process at the fission barrier, independent of initial $Y_e$ and entropy variations.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: fission_cycling_spectral_ablation comparing the predicted spectral absorption features of the third r-process peak shift and actinide signatures against models where fission cycling is disabled, while holding initial electron fraction and entropy distributions constant.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Spectral synthesis verification demonstrating that the derived abundance shifts match kilonova absorption features for the third peak and actinides, and are absent in the fission-ablated models, with initial electron fraction and entropy distributions held constant.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Kilonova spectral synthesis and multi-messenger observations of neutron star mergers, specifically targeting third-peak and actinide absorption features, controlling for initial ejecta conditions.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mechanism fails to produce observable peak shifts if the kilonova expansion rate is too rapid, or if initial electron fraction ($Y_e$) and entropy variations dominate the abundance patterns, restricting the validity domain to high-entropy dynamical ejecta with constrained initial conditions where fission cycling can complete before freeze-out.

directions.title: nuclear reactor kinetics
directions.abstract: Formulate the r-process fission cycling as a delayed neutron precursor problem, relaxing the standard instantaneous recycling assumption. We derive the conditions under which the beta-decay timescales of fission fragments act as dynamical precursors, regulating the neutron economy and final abundance patterns in neutron star merger wind ejecta.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The beta-decay and delayed neutron emission timescales of r-process fission fragments function as dynamical precursors that regulate fission recycling efficiency, analogous to delayed neutrons in reactor kinetics, provided the astrophysical expansion timescale is comparable to these decay timescales.

scientific_object.description: A formal mapping of the delayed neutron precursor equations (e.g., Inhour equation) to the r-process fission cycling network, treating fission fragments as formal precursor groups.

hypothesis.mechanism_or_relation: The target relation between the effective delayed neutron fraction of fission fragments and the r-process recycling efficiency, determining the final abundance peak formation.
hypothesis.intervention_or_transformation: Relaxation of the instantaneous fission recycling condition in r-process network equations to include time-dependent delayed neutron precursor source terms.
hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Fission fragments undergo beta decay with characteristic half-lives; a fraction of these decays result in neutron emission. These neutrons are re-captured on a timescale delayed relative to the initial fission event, altering the local neutron-to-seed ratio and the progression of the r-process.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: High-resolution spectroscopic identification of specific heavy element abundances (e.g., actinide-to-lanthanide ratios) in kilonova remnants that exhibit deviations from instantaneous recycling models, matching the precursor-inclusive abundance patterns.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Observation of specific heavy element abundance patterns (e.g., third r-process peak and actinide abundances) in kilonova ejecta to constrain the fission recycling efficiency and validate the delayed precursor timescales.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Based on established nuclear reactor kinetics formalism and theoretical r-process network models; relies on theoretical nuclear physics inputs (beta-decay half-lives, delayed neutron probabilities) for highly neutron-rich nuclei which carry significant theoretical uncertainty.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The formalism fails (counterexample boundary) in extremely rapid expansion scenarios (e.g., dynamical ejecta with rapid cooling) where the expansion timescale is orders of magnitude shorter than the beta-decay half-lives of the dominant fission fragments, making the delayed terms dynamically negligible.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Restricted to astrophysical environments with expansion timescales (milliseconds to seconds) comparable to the beta-decay half-lives of neutron-rich fission fragments (seconds to minutes), specifically applicable to the wind ejecta of neutron star mergers.
assumptions: The beta-decay half-lives and delayed neutron probabilities of highly neutron-rich fission fragments are non-negligible compared to the astrophysical expansion timescale.
The neutron capture cross-sections of the fission fragments are sufficiently large that emitted delayed neutrons are re-captured locally before escaping the ejecta.
The standard r-process network equations can be formally extended with source terms analogous to delayed neutron precursor groups in reactor kinetics.

directions.title: Fission-Driven Opacity Modulation in Kilonovae: Unifying 3D Ejecta Geometry and Delayed Neutron Recycling
directions.abstract: The origins of the heaviest elements rely on rapid neutron-capture and fission recycling in neutron star mergers, but current models struggle to reconcile viewing-angle dependencies with central engine fission dynamics. We introduce the Fission-Opacity Coupling Relation, unifying the geometric constraints of lanthanide curtaining with superheavy element fission timescales. By relaxing the assumption of instantaneous fission recycling, we derive how delayed neutron release alters the local electron fraction and lanthanide production in 3D ejecta at late times. This representation shift exposes a new invariant: the late-time viewing-angle dependent phase shift of the bolometric light curve, providing a direct observational signature to discriminate fission-driven nucleosynthesis from standard geometric asymmetries.

hypothesis.central_hypothesis: The delayed release of neutrons from the fission of superheavy elements (Z >= 92) systematically alters the local electron fraction in 3D kilonova ejecta, inducing a late-time viewing-angle dependent phase shift in the bolometric light curve that scales specifically with the fission recycling timescale, distinguishable from early-time geometric asymmetries.

hypothesis.expected_mechanism: Delayed neutron injection prolongs the r-process in specific geometric sectors of the ejecta at late times, increasing the lanthanide fraction and opacity locally. This creates anisotropic opacity that shifts the late-time light curve peak depending on the observer's viewing angle, distinct from early-time dynamical ejecta geometry.
hypothesis.discriminating_observation: Measurement of the late-time (t > 10 days) bolometric light curve phase shift and specific superheavy/lanthanide spectral absorption features across different viewing angles, which isolates the fission-delay signature from early-time standard r-process geometric models.
hypothesis.evidence_requirement: Multi-messenger observations of kilonovae providing late-time (t > 10 days) time-resolved spectroscopy and bolometric light curves at multiple viewing angles, or statistical inference from a population of events with known inclination angles.
hypothesis.evidence_basis: Observational evidence of strontium and lanthanide features in kilonova spectra (e.g., GW170817), combined with gravitational wave inclination angle measurements, provides the empirical foundation, though late-time superheavy features remain theoretically predicted.
hypothesis.boundary_or_failure_condition: The mechanism holds within the kilonova ejecta validity domain (ejecta masses ~0.01-0.05 M_sun, velocities 0.1-0.3c) at late times. It fails or becomes unidentifiable if the fission half-lives are too short (< milliseconds), if the ejecta is entirely spherically symmetric, or if early-time geometric asymmetries completely dominate the late-time light curve morphology.
hypothesis.claim_scope: Kilonova ejecta environments where superheavy element fission significantly contributes to the r-process abundance pattern, specifically isolating late-time (t > 10 days) bolometric light curve phase shifts that scale with fission recycling timescales, distinguishing them from early-time geometric asymmetries.

Local electron fraction (Ye) dictates lanthanide production and thus opacity.
Fission half-lives of relevant superheavy isotopes are sufficiently long (> milliseconds) to induce macroscopic geometric delays in neutron release at late times.
Early-time geometric asymmetries (e.g., dynamical vs. wind ejecta) can be observationally or theoretically decoupled from late-time fission-driven opacity changes.

directions.falsifier: Observation of kilonova late-time light curves showing no viewing-angle dependent phase shifts correlated with fission timescales, theoretical proof that superheavy fission half-lives are strictly < milliseconds, or demonstration that early-time geometric asymmetries fully account for all late-time viewing-angle dependencies.

directions.abstract: The origin of the heaviest elements relies on the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) in neutron star mergers, but simplified models often assume instantaneous fission neutron release, failing to capture the dynamics of the third r-process peak. directions.title: Fission Fragment Precursor Formalism: Relating Beta-Decay Timing to Recycling Efficiency in the Astrophysical r-Process
directions.abstract: The origins of heavy elements via the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) in neutron star mergers rely on fission cycling, yet standard models often assume instantaneous fission recycling. We apply a delayed neutron precursor formalism to r-process fission cycling, treating fission fragments as precursors whose beta-decay neutron release timing governs recycling efficiency. By replacing the weak assumption of instantaneous recycling with a refined precursor-recycling efficiency relation, we derive the fission cycling dynamics. We establish the validity domain for this reactor-kinetics analogy in astrophysical environments—specifically where the expansion timescale is comparable to precursor beta-decay half-lives—and propose a discriminating observation: the shift in specific isotopic ratios (e.g., actinide-to-lanthanide) within the integrated third r-process peak, which manifests macroscopically as a distinct change in lanthanide/actinide opacity. This isolates fission-driven temporal nucleosynthesis from alternative scenarios driven by initial condition variations or mass-model uncertainties.

This temporal effect alters the macroscopic lanthanide/actinide opacity in a predictable manner that is distinct from shifts caused by variations in initial ejecta conditions or nuclear mass model uncertainties, provided the expansion timescale falls within the derived validity domain.

trace.scientific_concern: The claim that time-dependent fission timescales 'directly dictate' third r-process peak shifts and viewing-angle opacities overstates the causal role of fission. Conflating the nucleosynthetic yield modulation with the primary hydrodynamic drivers of lanthanide curtaining risks misattributing the physical origin of the geometric spectral variations.

directions.title: Formal Derivation of Fission Neutron Release Timescales and Third r-Process Peak Shifts in Kilonovae
directions.abstract: The origins of heavy elements (Z >= 92) in neutron star mergers rely on the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process), but the precise role of fission recycling remains formally under-constrained. We replace the standard assumption of instantaneous fission recycling with a refined derivation that formally links finite fission neutron release timescales to observable shifts in the third r-process peak (A ~ 195) and actinide abundances. By unifying the nucleosynthesis constraint system with relaxed kilonova mechanism axioms, we construct a shared mechanism that isolates fission-driven nucleosynthesis. Crucially, we explicitly construct a counterexample boundary and uniqueness condition to ensure the predicted peak shifts remain non-degenerate with bulk thermodynamic variations (e.g., electron fraction and entropy), providing a strictly falsifiable boundary for heavy-element synthesis in relativistic outflows.
